title: Transactions, serializability and locking
subtitle: Many users, one database: how to interleave their work so the result is as if they had taken turns.

sections.title: Transactions and ACID
sections.body: A transaction is a sequence of operations that must be treated as one: transfer Rs 500 from A to B = read A, subtract, write A, read B, add, write B. The ACID properties: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (integrity rules hold before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other’s partial work), Durability (committed changes survive a crash).

questions.prompt: Money is debited from A but the system crashes before crediting B. Which property ensures the debit is undone?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is about surviving a crash after commit.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: All operations take effect or none do.

figures.caption: Figure 7.1.1 — transaction states
figures.note: Every transaction ends as committed or aborted.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
(Begin) as b
[Active] as a #blue
[Partially committed] as p #amber
[Committed] as c #mint
[Failed] as f #rose
[Aborted: rolled back] as x #rose
b -> a
a -> p : last operation done
p -> c : changes made durable
a -> f : error
p -> f : crash
f -> x : undo
@0 b -> a : start
@1 a -> p : finish
@2 p -> c : commit
loop 4");

sections.title: Problems with interleaving
sections.body: Without control, interleaved transactions cause: the lost update (two writes, one overwritten), the dirty read (reading another’s uncommitted value that is later rolled back), the unrepeatable read (two reads of one item differ) and the phantom (a repeated query finds new rows).

choices.text: Reading data written by a transaction that has not yet committed.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: If it rolls back, you acted on data that never existed.

figures.caption: Figure 7.2.1 — a lost update
figures.note: The second write overwrote the first.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[T1] as a
[Database item x] as x
[T2] as b
a -> x : read x (x = 100)
b -> x : write x = 50
a -> x : write x = 100 + 10
b -> b : T2’s update is lost");

sections.title: Conflict serializability
sections.body:
A serial schedule runs transactions one after another. An interleaved schedule is serializable if it is equivalent to a serial one. Two operations conflict if they are from different transactions, touch the same item and at least one is a write. Draw a precedence graph (edge Ti → Tj if a conflicting operation of Ti comes before Tj’s): the schedule is conflict-serializable exactly when the graph has no cycle, and a topological order gives the equivalent serial order.

r1(x) w2(x) w1(x): serializable no (edges T1->T2 T2->T1); r1(x) w1(x) r2(x) w2(x): yes — equivalent serial order T1 T2.

questions.prompt: A cycle in the precedence graph means…

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: A serial schedule has no interleaving.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each transaction must precede the other — impossible in any serial order.

figures.caption: Figure 7.3.2 — serializable
figures.note: Acyclic: equivalent to T1 then T2.
figures.script: var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"ok","engine":"serializability","schedule":"r1(x) w1(x) r2(x) w2(x)","width":600,"height":440});

problems.prompt: Is the schedule r1(x) w2(x) w1(x) conflict-serializable?
problems.answer: No. r1(x) before w2(x) gives T1→T2; w2(x) before w1(x) gives T2→T1 — a cycle. Checker: serializable = no.

sections.title: Locking and two-phase locking
sections.body: Transactions take shared (S, for reading) and exclusive (X, for writing) locks; S is compatible with S, X with nothing. Two-phase locking (2PL) guarantees serializability: a growing phase (only acquire locks) then a shrinking phase (only release). Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks to commit, which also prevents dirty reads and cascading aborts. Multiple granularity locks (database, table, page, row) with intention locks let a transaction lock coarsely or finely.

choices.text: No lock is acquired after the first lock is released.
Only two transactions at a time.

figures.caption: Figure 7.4.1 — exclusive lock blocks a reader
figures.note: T2 waits until T1 releases x.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[T1] as a
[Lock manager] as l
[T2] as b
a -> l : lock-X(x)
l --> a : granted
b -> l : lock-S(x)
l --> b : wait (x is locked)
a -> l : unlock(x) at commit
l --> b : granted");

sections.title: Deadlock
sections.body: T1 holds x and wants y; T2 holds y and wants x: deadlock. Detect it with a wait-for graph (a cycle means deadlock) and abort a victim. Prevention: impose a lock order, or use timestamps — wait–die (older waits, younger dies) and wound–wait (older wounds younger).

worked.why: T1 (timestamp 5) requests a lock held by T2 (timestamp 9). Wait–die: older may wait for younger.
Reverse: T2 (9) requests a lock held by T1 (5): the younger requester dies (aborts) and restarts with its old timestamp.

questions.prompt: A cycle in the wait-for graph indicates…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each transaction waits for another in the cycle.

sections.title: Isolation levels
sections.body: SQL defines four levels: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads possible), READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (no unrepeatable reads), SERIALIZABLE (no phantoms either). Stronger isolation means more waiting.

questions.prompt: Which level prevents dirty reads but allows unrepeatable reads?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: You see only committed data, but it can change between your reads.
